items.title: Taxes Are an Impact Strategy (Blog)
items.summary: More than an obligation, taxation contributes to the only systems ever shown to deliver essential services equitably and at scale. We love a good impact story. The story of the foundation that designed a new innovative environmental program. The entrepreneur that scaled a social innovation. The new catalytic capital fund. But I have spent enough time in this field to recognize that much of this work, for all its good intentions and often very real impact, can also end up preserving the status quo, or at least leaving it unchanged. That status quo is an economy capable of generating extraordinary wealth, yet one that continues to distribute it so unevenly that large parts of society are being left behind, with the most vulnerable furthest behind of all. It is also an economy generating growing frustration and discontent with how it works, and for whom. This means that, sometimes, the most impactful thing many of us can do is simply to pay our taxes. It also means that encouraging, advocating for, and supporting adequate taxation might be the most important thing the social sector as a whole can put its energy into. Saying this can feel almost too simple. Yet much of the impact sector operates on the understanding that governments often face severe resource and operational constraints when addressing complex social and environmental issues. As a result, private capital is naturally expected to bridge the divide, with foundations serving as crucial catalysts and conveners. This framework is widely recognized as the “Sustainable Development Goals funding gap.”

items.title: AI and Nonprofit Strategic Independence (Blog)
items.summary: Why now is the moment for nonprofits to build and customize their own mission-critical technology, and three steps to getting started. Seven years ago, Becky Straw co-founded The Adventure Project, a nonprofit that works to create jobs in Africa. She was not a computer programmer, so she paid a developer $7,000 to create a website using the application Webflow. For years, she wanted to embed a customized map feature on the homepage using Mapbox to show where the organization was making progress, but she didn’t have the funds to afford more development. Earlier this year, funding to hire a developer became irrelevant. Straw didn’t know any more about website developing and coding than she did seven years earlier, but Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude did, and she used it to create the code she needed to embed Mapbox herself. For decades, nonprofits have been beholden to commercial software companies and developers—and more recently, software as a service (SaaS) companies—to manage and support infrastructure essential to core operations. This created expensive trade-offs, including vendor lock-in, price increases, limited customization, dependence on commercial roadmaps, and occasional break down, like when the fundraising company Flipcause went bankrupt and left organizations scrambling to replace it. AI-powered coding tools are challenging the stranglehold that software companies have traditionally had over nonprofits. Some people are calling this moment the SaaS-pocalypse. I call it Strategic Independence Day.

items.title: The Power of Labels
items.summary: Health-climate warning labels at gas pumps are gaining political momentum as research shows they can shift consumer attitudes away from fossil fuels. Since 2020, gas pumps in Cambridge, Massachusetts, have displayed a label that says, Warning: Burning gasoline, diesel and ethanol has major consequences on human health and on the environment including contributing to climate change. Most residents of the town famous for harboring Harvard University and MIT already support stronger action on climate change. In fact, across the political spectrum, majorities nationwide express concern about the health and climate harms of continued fossil-fuel use. Health-climate warning labels, often called “warming labels,” are notices placed on gas pumps that inform consumers about the health and environmental consequences of burning fossil fuels. In practice, however, they may do less to warn consumers than to remind them, each time drivers fill their tanks, that concern about the harms of fossil-fuel use is widely shared. By making that concern visible, warming labels can help establish a social expectation that people should consider cleaner alternatives to gasoline and diesel whenever possible. Over time, that expectation could help drive a broader cultural shift away from fossil fuels.

items.title: Education Needs Impact Engineering
items.summary: The many discoveries from education research aren't making it to the classroom. It should follow the medical model of building infrastructure to translate research into impact. In 2003, the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) declared that medical research was failing patients. Decades of brilliant basic science sat stranded in academic journals while people suffered from treatable diseases. The problem wasn’t a lack of discovery; it was a lack of translation. The relevant scientific insights existed, but the infrastructure to move them from the lab to bedside did not. The solution was translational medicine, a new discipline supported by an ecosystem of specialized infrastructure—clinical-trial-design firms, regulatory navigators, data-management systems, and manufacturing expertise. Researchers didn’t build this infrastructure themselves, but their access to it transformed medical practice.
